criterion: The verdicts it produces are identical to the pairwise version for every ordering, including sessions whose bounds are missing or reversed
summary: Held by a test rather than argued. The pairwise implementation is written out in tests.test_conformance_contract.ContestedEquivalenceTests as the specification and the two are compared: test_the_narrowed_search_agrees_with_comparing_every_pair over 500 generated groups, and test_it_agrees_whatever_order_the_sessions_arrive_in over every permutation of a five-session group, because the pairwise version could not depend on arrival order and a sorted sweep can. The window pool is chosen for the cases a reader would not think to try: one missing its start, one missing its end, one missing both, one whose end precedes its start, two identical windows, and two touching only at an endpoint. Equivalence is also structural, not just measured: the predicate still has one implementation - the sweep hands its chosen candidate to _overlaps rather than re-deriving the comparison - and the candidate is the one reaching furthest within the prefix, which is exactly the maximum over the only free half of the predicate, since every candidate already satisfies the other. Two ends are tracked so a session is never compared against itself, and a session missing a bound is left out of the ordering, which is what the pairwise version did by answering False for every pair involving one.
